preamble: Tensing of the near-close [ɪ] to close [i]. In English happy-tensing, a final unstressed i-type vowel, as in happy, city, coffee and money, is tense [i] rather than lax [ɪ]; it is now found in most dialects of English and is uniform in South African, Australian and New Zealand English. Jack Windsor Lewis held that the British vowel moved from [i] to [ɪ] in the second quarter of the 19th century and returned to [i] in non-conservative British accents towards the last quarter of the 20th century.

examples.note: Tensing also applies to inflected forms such as cities and hurried, and to clitic me, he and she (show me, would he?).

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Phonological history of English close front vowels. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_history_of_English_close_front_vowels
